citations.claim: 99% of surveyed organizations actively use Java
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="2-9">Of all businesses contacted globally to participate in the Azul 2025 State of Java Survey & Report, only 1% of respondents were disqualified from taking the survey because they did not use Java in their enterprise—highlighting that 99% of organizations surveyed actively use Java.</cite>

citations.claim: Nearly 70% of respondents run more than half their applications on Java/JVM
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="3-1">Azul's 2025 State of Java Survey found 99% of surveyed organizations actively use Java, and nearly 70% reported that more than half of their applications are built with Java or run on the JVM.</cite>

citations.claim: Netflix runs thousands of Java microservices on Azul Zulu OpenJDK in production
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="21-1,21-2,21-3">Contrary to popular belief, Netflix doesn't have its own JVM. They're just using the Azul Zulu JVM which is an OpenJDK build. Overall, Netflix has around 2800 Java applications that are mostly microservices of varying sizes.</cite>

citations.claim: A financial institution ran a decade-plus Java modernization/production engagement
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="3-4">One financial institution partnered with Keyhole across multiple phases from 2011 to 2025, modernizing COBOL-based batch processing with Spring Batch and continuing to invest in the platform for more than a decade thus far.</cite>

citations.claim: Java professional usage share is near the top of enterprise languages in a large independent survey
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="42-4,42-5">In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 29.4% of all respondents said they had done extensive work in Java over the past year, on a question answered by 31,771 people. Among professional developers the figure was 29.6%, just behind C# at 29.9%.</cite>

citations.claim: Java's production role in mission-critical banking/insurance/telecom systems
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="6-5">Millions of lines of production code power the world's banks, insurance companies, healthcare systems, and government agencies.</cite>

findings.enterprise_survey_evidence: An independent annual industry survey of 2,000+ Java professionals found that the overwhelming majority of surveyed organizations actively use Java in production and that a majority run more than half of their applications on the JVM.
findings.industry_breadth: Public sources point to production Java usage concentrated in regulated, high-scale sectors (financial services and insurance, telecom, banking) with multi-decade running production systems, plus a documented case of a financial institution's decade-plus modernization program targeting the Java platform.
findings.named_production_deployment: Netflix operates thousands of Java-based microservices in production, and its engineering blog documents the specific application count and JVM choice (Azul Zulu OpenJDK build).
findings.professional_usage_share: An independent large-scale developer survey (49,000+ respondents) found Java professional usage nearly tied with the second-highest non-JavaScript enterprise language.

metric.production_adoption_deployment_ev.limitations: The Azul survey is vendor-sponsored (Azul sells Java runtime/support products), which may skew respondent recruitment toward existing Java shops; this is disclosed and cross-checked against an independent, non-Java-vendor source (Stack Overflow Developer Survey) and a named first-party engineering disclosure (Netflix) rather than relied on alone. Netflix was fixed as the named case study before evidence collection per the declared selection rule and is not the only company with public Java production evidence, but is used consistently as the anchor case for this work unit.

predeclared_sampling.candidate_universe: Named companies with public Java engineering disclosures include Netflix, LinkedIn, Amazon, Google, Uber, and large financial institutions; Netflix was selected as the fixed target because it publishes the most detailed, quantified, and recurring public disclosures of Java application counts and JVM tuning practices.
predeclared_sampling.retrieval_route: Web search snapshot, same single retrieval route and 2-query depth used for the paired third-party-tool metric in this work unit.
predeclared_sampling.selection_rule: Use one externally observable, methodology-independent large-scale industry adoption survey with a fixed, repeated methodology (Azul's annual State of Java Survey & Report, 2,000+ respondents) as the primary quantitative source, cross-checked with one named-company engineering case study (Netflix Technology Blog / ByteByteGo summary of Netflix's Java usage) selected because Netflix is one of the most extensively documented public production deployments of Java at scale and its engineering blog is a first-party, language-neutral selection criterion (largest public tech-company engineering blog with dedicated Java-usage disclosures), plus one labor-market indicator (Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey professional usage share) for triangulation.

metric.production_adoption_deployment_ev.score_rationale: Independent survey data (99% enterprise usage, ~70% majority-JVM application share), a large, well-documented named hyperscale production deployment (Netflix, ~2,800 Java microservices), decade-plus enterprise modernization case evidence, and near-top-tier professional usage share in an independent, non-vendor developer survey together constitute strong, multi-source production adoption evidence, supporting a near-maximum normalized score.

citations.claim: IntelliJ IDEA leads Java IDE usage
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="12-5">IntelliJ IDEA is the most popular Java IDE in 2026, used by 84% of Java developers according to the 2025 Java Developer Productivity Report.</cite> <cite index="12-6">VS Code ranks second at 31%, followed by Eclipse at 28%.</cite>

citations.claim: Three IDEs cover the large majority of the market
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="11-4">Eclipse, IntelliJ IDEA and NetBeans...comfortably take up over 90% of the IDE market.</cite>

citations.claim: Static analysis tools integrate with Maven/Gradle build pipelines
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="28-1,28-2">Setup involves connecting a Java project to SonarQube Cloud and configuring Maven or Gradle to trigger analysis during the build process...SonarQube Cloud analyzes Java pull requests and branches, surfacing bugs, vulnerabilities, and code smells</cite>

citations.claim: PMD integrates tightly and quickly into Maven/Gradle builds as an alternative/complementary static analyzer
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="31-3,31-18">PMD runs as part of your Maven or Gradle build...PMD 7.x (released in 2024) supports Java 21, runs across 16 languages, and gives teams access to hundreds of battle-tested Java rules</cite>

citations.claim: Multiple additional static-analysis tools are used together via Gradle/Maven plugins
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="32-5,32-8">I am mostly working with Java and Gradle, or Maven...I implemented Violations Gradle Plugin (and also Violations Maven Plugin) that you can configure to parse the report files of your tools</cite>

citations.claim: Large-scale operators build on-host Java profiling using standard JDK tooling (jstack) alongside custom tooling
citations.quote_evidence: <cite index="20-2,20-3">a flamegraph generated by sampling the on-host Java process using jstack. This view allows an engineer to quickly drill on where the Java process is spending CPU time.</cite>

findings.build_tools: Maven and Gradle are the two dominant, actively maintained Java build/dependency-management tools, both with first-class integration into IDEs and static-analysis tools.
findings.ide_landscape: IDE adoption is dominated by JetBrains IntelliJ IDEA, with VS Code and Eclipse as strong secondary options, and NetBeans as a smaller but still-supported option.
findings.static_analysis_debugging_profiling: Multiple independently maintained static-analysis tools (SonarQube/SonarCloud, PMD, Checkstyle) integrate directly into Maven/Gradle builds and CI pipelines, and the JDK ships built-in production diagnostics (Java Flight Recorder, jstack, jcmd) supplemented by third-party profilers (JProfiler, YourKit, async-profiler) and monitoring agents (as used at Netflix for on-host flamegraph generation via jstack).

metric.third_party_tool_availability.limitations: IDE/build-tool percentages come from an opt-in vendor survey (JRebel/Perforce) and general market-analysis blogs rather than a single authoritative census; figures vary across sources (e.g., IntelliJ share cited as 33%-84% depending on survey year/methodology) and are used only as one input alongside documented first-party tool-integration evidence, not as the sole basis for the score.

predeclared_sampling.candidate_universe: All Java IDEs/tools appearing in the JRebel 2025 Java Developer Productivity Report (IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code, Eclipse, NetBeans, JetBrains Fleet) plus the standard Java build tools (Maven, Gradle, Ant) and static analysis tools (SonarQube/SonarCloud, PMD, Checkstyle, SpotBugs/Findbugs) referenced in official SonarSource/PMD documentation.
predeclared_sampling.retrieval_route: Web search snapshot, single retrieval route (general web search), same depth (2 queries) as used for the paired production-adoption metric in this work unit.
predeclared_sampling.selection_rule: Examine a fixed, language-neutral tool-category checklist (IDE, build/dependency tool, static analysis/linter, debugger, profiler, CI/CD integration) using externally observable, methodology-independent sources: a public developer-productivity survey with a fixed methodology (Perforce/JRebel 2025 Java Developer Productivity Report) for IDE share, and official/first-party tool documentation (SonarSource docs, PMD project docs) for static-analysis integration, cross-checked against a general market-research summary (GeeksforGeeks) and one industry blog comparison (dev.to). This checklist and route set is applied identically for every language in this ecosystem work stream.

metric.third_party_tool_availability.score_rationale: Java has multiple mature, independently maintained, actively updated options in every core tool category (2+ dominant full-featured IDEs plus VS Code support, 2 dominant build tools, 3+ static-analysis tools with native build-system plugins, built-in JDK production diagnostics plus commercial/OSS profilers, and first-class CI/CD plugin support for Jenkins/GitHub/GitLab). This breadth and maturity across every category supports a near-maximum normalized score.
